author: @billpaliwoda5012
comment:
Why are you so overwrought about the key card?  First, it's a backup, your phone is your primary key.  Second, to unlock the door all you need do it place it under the side pillar camera as outlined in the user's manual...no "hunting" for the right spot needed.  Finally, to start the car all you do is place it behind the cup holders and press the brake pedal, then you put it away.  Since the car never moves during this start procedure the key card will never slide around.  Beats the hell out of carrying around a $300-$400 fob that many luxury cars come with.   

You can set the speed of your wipers via voice command without using the screen (i.e., "Set wipers to level 3" or "Turn wipers off").  Much more expensive cars don't have this feature.  In fact you can control many of the settings for the car via voice commands.

Regarding braking, when using regen braking when the car comes to a stop it applies the regular brakes to hold the car still, not the parking brake.

When using cruise control you can set the following distance based on seconds behind the car in front of you, not how many car lengths (at least that's the way it works in the US)

comment: Good video and mainly informative with some interesting points, but i felt you were not grasping the 'whole EV experience'.  Is 6 months enough time to get into the mindset?  I have been driving EV's for well over 2 years and frankly loved every vehicle i have driven, and its been quite a few.  So, Kia EV6 lovely car, Hyundai Ioniq 5, still a stunning design and so spacious inside, Polestar 2, odd seating with a large centre console that makes the driving position cramped, VW ID.3 & 4 simply stunning and the Cupra Born (basically an ID.3 but takes the looks and design to the next step).  Mercedes EQA, B and C are again lovely but lack in range somewhat and then the BMW iX40 - stunning to look at and a music sound system to die for, but on the 40 sadly lacking range.  Each EV stands alone with quirks, but they all rely on a charging infrastructure which is sadly lacking in some areas such as Wales, or to be more precise Mid-Wales.  My favourite car is a toss up between the Tesla Model 3 Long Range AWD and the BMW iX40 Xdrive, as they both have their strengths.  Both are very minimalistic when it comes to actual controls and buttons, but for sheer comfort the BMW iX wins hands down but for range the Tesla Model 3 LR, plus the Tesla Supercharger network is fantastic and so much cheaper per kW that any i have used and they seem to be expanding many sites and increasing numbers.  I was in Rugby Moto services around 8 months ago where there were 12x Gridserve 350kWh chargers and 12x Tesla Superchargers - last week running that way again, there are now 28x Tesla Chargers.  Safe driving everyone

author: @fredturk6447
comment:
As a current model 3 owner I think improving the suspension is a great step forward. The current suspension is great in that the car does not roll into corners, however, with tyres at their pressure rating the ride is harsh (reduce tyre pressure a little to improve).  The suspension also can thump a bit if it hits a bump in the road. However, having said that, overall it is a great car to drive with responsive steering and amazing acceleration. 
The bad things are no foot room in the back seat, dumb external door handles, seats that while reasonable are not as comfortable as a BMW 3 series seat, bad positioning of window controls on the driver side door causing accidental opening of rear window, cheap carpet material, not enough sound deadening for road noise, should have a HUD for speed and status info, and the multi functionality of the right hand stalk can be a problem (if you have just been driving a vehicle with the turn indicator on the right and want to turn left in the Tesla accidentally pushing the right stalk up at low speed it will put you in reverse, which is not such a good idea).   Oh and while I am at it the whole way the door opens with a push button, but still has an emergency release handle seems pointless and should be redesigned.
The there is autopilot, which although a great benefit a lot of the time has serious limitations. This is not FSD but as a taste of FSD it does not inspire confidence.  I won’t go through all the issues here, but based on my own experience driving an Australian version it can cause accidents with a tendency to jam on the brakes too soon and too often.

author: @Grand_Priest_Goku
comment:
great video, but regarding your remark about how "most EVs tend to run out of steam at higher speeds", that's not really a problem with EVs, it's a problem with their transmission. Most manufacturers don't bother putting multi-speed transmissions on EVs because profit-wise it's not worth it, so they usually just put a single short final drive ratio. This means that the car maxes out the motor's rpm way too soon, and is only limited by motor spin speed rather than power. Given them another gear or a longer final drive ratio and they'll easily get higher top speed. If you aren't convinced, just look at how high the top speeds of EV bullet trains are compared to steam or even diesel-electric locomotives. Electric is literally meant for top speed.

Edit: forgot to mention that current EV cars are only using permanent magnet DC motors rather than the AC motors on bullet trains. AC motors have constant torque so the hp just keeps increasing as the rpm increases and can reach some extreme numbers

author: @boba7039
comment:
I want to talk about a number of points made during the presentation. 

Stainless steel body panel - They sound great on paper but in reality, they do not work. Over the last couple of years, we have heard that they will not dent.  You can dent the panel by hitting it along the outside edge or on a crease. If you scratch the panel, you can try sanding it out, but then you have a blotch. If the Cybertruck is a couple of years old and you replace a panel, it will NOT match the others as the old panels will be slightly different shade.  Pictures of pre-production Cybertruck in use show lots of fingerprints around all the doors and tailgate. In the video they show a side impact test that all vehicles have to pass in order to be sold in the US. If you look at the doors after the impact, you will see the outside stainless steel skin on both doors is clearly bent. Infact the entire diver's door is bent. This is to be expected after a hit like that. 

Bullet proof doors - The bullets they used are soft point bullets propelled at sub sonic speeds. When they hit the door they mushroom and splinter (disturbing the impact over a wider area) as shown in the high speed photograph. A better test would have been to use Full Metal Jacket FMJ bullets in calibers that would propel them at supersonic speed. In any case the stainless steel door skin would do better than traditional metal door skins, but I would not call the Cybertruck bullet proof. 

Truck bed - The biggest complaints about the first-generation Honda Ridgeline was the rear quarter sail panels. You could not reach over the side to get something out of the bed. That's why the second-generation Ridgeline does not have sail panels. So why does the Cybertruck have sail panels? What a huge mistake. In the video they show loading a number of different things in the bed. I would like to see someone make a ladder rack for long ladders, lumber, pipe, etc. that would not interfere with the loading/unloaded large items from the bed (I doubt it can be done). Which would mean that the Cybertruck has limitations that other trucks don't have. 

Air ride suspension - Which gives the Cybertruck a smooth ride. Air Ride Suspension is standard equipment on the Hummer EV truck and optional on RAM trucks for many years now.

4 wheel steering - The GMC Hummer EV has 4 wheel steering. GM had this technology way before Tesla was ever thought of. Quadrasteer is the name of a four wheel steering system developed by Delphi Automotive while under the ownership of General Motors for use in automobiles. It was available as an option on GM's full-size pickup trucks and 2500 Suburban's for model years 2002 through 2005.

Armor Glass - Which is shatter resistant. In the video they throw a baseball at the window instead of a large ball baring like they did at the Cybertruck introduction. Nor did they shoot bullets at the glass.

Sled pull - In the video they showed a sled pulling competition on dirt with some of their competitors. Notice they left out the GMC Hummer EV. I wonder why? Since this competition is being done on dirt, 4 wheel drive and the type of tires each truck has will make a huge difference on how they each one does. The Cybertruck had tires will a large block tread vs the competitors had street tires. NOT a fair competition at all!

Drag strip race with a Porsche 911 - There are 25 different versions of the 911, which one where they using? They never tell you. Yes, the Cybertruck was pulling a trailer with another 911 on it and won the race. Big deal. Let's use the 911 GT2RS and the Cybertruck doesn't have to pull a trailer and let's see what happens. 

320 to 340 miles range - There is supposedly a range extender that will increase range to 440 miles. But Tesla has provided no information. What happened to 500 miles range?

48 Volt system - Now this is the most revolutionary thing about the Cybertruck. Automakers have been talking about moving from 12 volts to 48 volts electrical systems starting in the 1990's. But no one wanted to be first because the cost for all the new 48 volt components (lights, controllers, computers, display screens, infotainment systems, etc.) would cost more than the 12 volt components. Now that Tesla has made the move all the others will make the transition over the next 5 to 8 years.

author: @gregkramer5588
comment:
I have to provide a counter point. The tone of this video is far from objective.  The intro makes it clear what the bias is. 
1. EV sales in CA, down to 21.3%. This is still a healthy number and year over year growth was still good. Nationwide it was 46% according to COX.  In regards to the "proposed mandate" 21.6% in 2023 with a 20% compound growth rate gets them to 100% in 2032.  BTW this "mandate" allows for 20% of it to be PHEVs. 
2. The idea that chargers are getting more common and more reliable is spun to imply this is a negative. "it seems the EV charging structure is getting worse".  This is not born out by any information on growth and improvements vs. sales. The joint venture between BMW, General Motors, Honda, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, and Stellantis and the roll out of their network is not even mentioned. 
3. Tesla sales are down which is extrapolated to be bad for EVs than when it is shown that others are growing it gets completely blown off as if it is not worth mentioning. 
4. The second section focuses on PHEVs, which I think are great BTW.  But the implication is that they are a competitor to EVs more than ICE vehicles.  This premise seems suspect but I do not have numbers. 
5. Mineral mining. The expert from Tokyo, which is far from an unbiased source BTW.  The expert fails to mention that ~90% of the minerals in EV batteries can be recovered and reused.  He also does not mention that LFP batteries usage is growing fast which changes his numbers by a huge amount for rare earth metals and lastly ignores the advancements that are happening in the battery industry. The oil extraction business is completely ignored as a comparison. 
6. Number of kilometers driving required to have a net break even for CO2.  This still does not take in to account recycling or LFP batteries and lets face it no electricity network uses 0 renewables.  Even then we are looking at 32k to 70k break even, which BTW is still a net positive since cars last way longer than that. 
7. GM will need to compete with the Ramcharger which is a PHEV which I believe is a real threat for them. I do not understand why more PHEVs would be spun as a negative for EVs.
8. The dealers!  So it starts with the 80% do not want an EV statement.  Well if sales are a 8% nation wide and 55% are saying not interested does that still not say that demand is growing? The tone once again is; people do not want EVs. Then it goes in to the generic Biden/government is bad in peoples opinion. Nothing here unique to the auto industry. Dealers do not want to change, install more equipment, or make less money on maintenance and train people for a new paradigm. This in a business that is driven by monthly sales!  Holy crap that is not shocking or even news IMO. 
9. Polestar and stripper name! This made me laugh.  I have known about Polestar for years but this never popped in to my head!  Anyway for sure it is hard to establish a new company and branding. When the Polestar 2 came here there was way less competition.  The interior space is just not great in this car when I sat in it. 
10. Vinfast, they are not ready for primetime for sure.  But let's face it many companies take years to really get going, even Tesla! 
11. Range, I would like ~300 miles but I do road trip more than average. The advancements in battery technology will make it easy to get the range option you want. Charging at home is key. To me it looks like average range is going up about 20% over the next 5 years. Which is great but even more important battery cost will come down a similar amount. 

Kirk if you want to do this every week I think that is great but if it is so slanted it will either fail or narrow your audience.

author: @ChrisWhalenCPA
comment:
Electric Vehicles, or EVs, Are Not Cars

The government and auto industry wants us to believe that EVs are interchangeable with gas-powered vehicles.

EVs are not a “car” as we know them. EVs are experimental transportation devices that the government wants us to accept as a car replacement.

I believe the rollout of them was extremely premature. They look like cars, and seem to function like cars, but they are not cars.

Words and their traditional definitions matter.

Using the word car for an EV is misleading. I try to avoid it.

EVs are a completely different machine and when purchasing one that should be our mindset.

Replacements For Vital Machines (Evs For Cars) Must Outperform Their Predecessors To Be Universally Adopted

For a new product or invention, which an EV is, to replace a tried and true significant part of our daily lives, like our cars, it has to be a better choice.

Do EVs outperform cars in all important areas?
How should a car replacement be better?
1) Cheaper purchase price, lifetime maintenance and disposal.
2) Better performance, road handling and driving range.
3) As many or more locations to “refuel” and lower recharging times than refueling. Overall more convenient and time saving than gas powered vehicles.
4) Safer in all ways, including charging away from home.
5) Seamless and transparent replacement for our current experience with cars.
6) EVs should be less expensive to insure.
7) End of Life Disposal must be cheaper and more environmentally friendly.


How do EVs stack up in those five categories?
1) EVs are more expensive than gas-powered vehicles. Overall costs over time are much higher for EVs. Even if they were cheaper, the current negative impacts of the loss of convenience and functionality make EVs not worth replacing our cars with experimental replacements. Government subsidies paid to corporations and individuals approach $50,000 per EV. An EV is less functional, yet more expensive? Who thought of this great system?
2) EVs have much higher average horsepower, but other than that the driving experience is not much different and is sometimes deficient. Range anxiety is real and total miles available on a full charge falls terribly behind a full tank of gas.
3) Gas stations are much safer and more convenient than EV charging stations. On the road charging can average ten times longer than refueling with gasoline. EVs fail miserably here.
4) The level of danger using an unmanned EV charging station at night in a deserted parking lot is not tenable, compared to gas stations which have personnel, lights and security cameras. EV battery explosions are commonplace.
5) EVs are not a cheaper, more functional replacement for our cars.
6) A true car replacement would be cheaper to insure. Middle class families already can’t afford car insurance.
7) EV End of Life Disposal? Is there even a plan? What is the tested process for dismantling and disposing of the dead batteries? I am sure this will be very costly for the unfortunate consumer who is the last owner.

EVs fail on almost every measure.

This certainly does not make a great case for EVs.

Using EVs dramatically changes your entire driving experience, one of the most important parts of our daily lives.

There are so many unanswered questions about the impact on us if the government were to ban gas-powered vehicles in favor of EVs.

Mandating EVs will change our way of life.

As with other government experiments in the recent past, they want us to be the test subjects.

I propose we opt out of this government experiment and all others in the future.

Fad For Wealthier People

EVs are still a fad for wealthier people for the most part. Currently they are mostly an option for owners of free standing single family homes and less often owners of townhouses with a garage.

And even for those free standing single family homeowners, once you have more than one EV, it can quickly become impractical, cumbersome and unworkable.

There are government laws forcing apartment complex owners and townhouse communities to allow residents to install charging stations, but they are not widely used.

The vast majority of renters and townhouse owners don’t have the ability to purchase an EV as they can’t charge them nightly.

EVs require access to a power supply that can extend to your EV where they are parked overnight. While away from home needing a charge, you need to find a charging station.

For people who own free standing homes, with a traditional garage and driveway setup, this is relatively simple and most practical. But even then, a family with two or more EVs may not be able to charge all of them overnight. Once you expand beyond one EV, things begin to fall apart.

Many townhouse owners are in the same predicament as apartment renters.
Renters of any type of home usually don’t have the ability or finances to install the systems needed to charge an EV. They would also need permission from the landlord.

Even if an apartment complex or townhouse association installed a few, having this done on mass scale for all apartment and townhouse residents is not practical for decades to come, if at all.

Townhouses, although purchased as a residence, are more likely to be a temporary stop to a free standing home, and so installing a charging station may not be worth the investment.

Excluding these drivers will stall or make impossible the complete replacement of gas-powered vehicles with EVs. 

So, what percentage of drivers are in free standing single family homes? This is the true market for EVs on the consumer level. And, again, only for one EV in the family.

Let’s take a look at the figures below.

It will tell us what % of us have severe barriers to entering the EV space.

132,000,000 (A) - USA Households			            	
83,000,000 (B) - Detached single family homes						
49,000,000 (C=A -B) - USA Households With Barriers To Entry Into EV Space	                
37.12% (D=C/A) - % USA Households With Barriers To Entry Into EV Space
233,000,000 (E) - Drivers In The USA			
86,000,000	(D×E) - USA Drivers With Barriers To Entry Into EV Space			

86,000,000 out of 233,000,000 U.S. drivers cannot practically transition to EV use. 

This 37% of drivers who cannot use an EV is important to remember, as it impacts the rest of the problems EV owners face.

Safety Issues At Charging Stations On The Road

Again, remember, we are imagining a world where gasoline is no longer needed and so gas stations would become a novelty.

So, with only EVs in everyday use, there will be times we need to charge away from home. Where will this take place? There is some EV charging infrastructure built out, but there are many problems. And this is with a very small percentage of EVs on the road.

Imagine, again, that only EVs were allowed. The infrastructure needed is unfathomable.

And what is the infrastructure for remote charging going to look like?

I have serious concerns here as should you.

When we need gas, we simply find an open gas station.

Gas stations have security cameras and personnel when they are open.

We take these well lit locations with employees and security cameras for granted. These safety features do not exist at EV charging locations. Most will be in parking lots of retail shopping centers with no attendants.

This decreases security and increases waiting times.  That is what they are proposing. We should not accept these severe regressions of course. 

Parents, let me ask you. Would you accept your children going into dark and empty parking lots, when retail stores are closed, to charge up for 20 or 30 minutes by themselves with no personnel on site?

comment:
Since this video talks about california, lets look at cali.  

at an average of 26-33 cents per kwh cost (assuming home only charging) every 60kwh costs about $16-20.  assuming 3.75whpm in the real world use (3.75 miles per kwh if im correct) would be 225 miles, some EVs are as low as 3.0 whpm which means your costs can be higher.  we will assume for this comparison, that the EV is operating in an optimal climate (not extreme cold) for these numbers.    
real california cost average is 33c per kwh.  so this estimate would actually be considered too low.
but for comparison, im using 60kwh vs a 10 gallon tank.    
a hybrid car that gets 45 miles per gallon, at $4.50 a gallon would cost $45 for 10 gallons, and 450 miles per 10 gallons. (the prius has a 10 gallon tank, and gets over 50mpg, but i lowballed it on purpose)
the EV would have to be charged 2x for the same/similar range, $36-40 on the low end estimate to go the same range.

a hybrid refuels in 5 minutes, an EV takes, at home, 6-30 hours (depending on charger type), and in public charging 25-40 minutes assuming its not full, or waiting time.  

now lets talk about public charger costs, which are higher than residential.  so those that use or need public charging, will cost 1.50-2x more than residential rates.  which means charging 60kwh to go 225 average miles will cost someone $30-$40, or $60-$80 compared to a 45mpg hybrid car costing $45-50 to refuel.  

then theres insurance, for some its 2x higher than a gas car.  

So where is the real benefit of EV compared to a better mpg hybrid in a place like california?  the costs to operate daily would run pretty similar, and give an owner far more freedom with a hybrid.   in cali, often the chargers are backed up too since they got so popular and i think potential owners are seeing this and backing off.  

Average range of 270 miles as you stated in the video for most EVs, is only in OPTIMAL climates (30F-95F).  we all know cold reduces 10-40% depending on how cold it is.  at 28F i lost less than 10%.  what they dont tell you is when its over 105F outside your range tanks as well, loss of 25-40% depending on habits and temps over 110F as over 110F it is even more reduced.  
California urban areas generally are within optimal climate or minimal outside of it, but traffic may reduce that range as well.

EV haters in these comments never fail to amaze me with their lack of comprehension of data, or unwillingness to represent it properly.

I’m sure you’ll get a lot of likes on this video from the anti-EV trolls, but you’re not properly representing data. Look at YOY increases and market share increases, not from one quarter to the next. Sales naturally increase and decline for some things at different parts of the year. Compare one entire year to another or the same quarter from different years to properly evaluate. You also have to look at market share, not just pure numbers, in case there’s an overall decline in vehicle sales that you’re not accounting for. I don’t think you’re being intentionally misleading, but it’s likely that the sources you’re citing are trying to make it seem like things are worse for EVs than they actually are. author: @markcoopers1930
comment:
19:50 from people I've talked too there's confusion on the best case for PHEVs here in the NE. Most want to do *all* day-to day activities in EV, incuding a work commute, but enjoy the reassurance of a gas motor on long trips or the occasional road trip. These people are upset at only 30-40 miles of EV range, when in reality they should probably just be getting a full EV (keep in mind 40 miles can take you through 20 towns and almost halfway across a state up here). 

Others want to use it just as a hybrid and never plug it in, never manage the esave/ev mode depending on where they are: they should just be getting ICE or a standard hybrid instead of hauling around a wasted plugin powertrain. Even as it regens itself its not nearly as efficient or cost effective as plugging in at home.

The understanding of the EV range being for city driving conditions where ICE motors are more stressed and less efficient is lost on people, and yet it's more appealing than the simpler switch to EV because of that safety net. This confusion seems like the best opportunity for range extended EVs like the Clarity to come back into the mix (refreshed for the modern age). Have people get the EV driving they want, the reassurance of a gas tank and the opportunity for plugging in and saving, and then let the cars' computer figure out when to burn gas to keep it going rather than the user.

As far as regulators: as always has been and always will be its the lobbyists, party platforms, and the re-election campaign posturing/ political games which actually choose what legislation gets passed. author: @minerran
comment:
This is not even a question of what people want .... I would love to have a 100% electric vehicle.  Its about what is practical.  Currently available rechargeable battery technology is not sufficient for a fully electric vehicle that matches the usability of an internal combustion vehicle (ICE). Also the power grid and typical home wiring is also not ready for the massive charging current demands that widespread use of such vehicles would result in.  In addition to all that, electric vehicles are not price competitive with ICE vehicles and government subsidies or tax breaks can't remedy that.  The only available solution is to migrate to more fuel efficient and cleaner burning ICE vehicles.  Hybrids can help this although they use the same inadequate battery technology.  I owned a Honda Civic Hybrid and was very disappointed in it, eventually having to trade it in when the battery pack went bad at 35K miles right after the warranty expired.  Was going to be about 1/5 the cost of a brand new vehicle to get a refurbished battery.  No thanks.

Right now, electric vehicles are only practical for owners who drive less that around 30 miles per day and have access to a charging station at work and at home or drive very infrequently.   For long trips or long daily commuting to work, it simply takes too long to recharge them.

author: @MrExplion
comment:
The best EV Nio!!! 
Base on fast charging car batteries just degrades the battery just like your mobile phone. Eventually the battery degrades so much, the car loses its value if you can’t swap out the battery. Replacing the batteries is tedious and expensive. Battery swapping centralizes battery management, so health is always maintained by the company, and in theory your EV could last forever.

Plus, you can always swap out different battery sizes. If you needed to make a 1000km journey, you could just swap out to a larger battery for a day or two, which is much more cost effective than buying a permanent 1000km range battery that you’ll only use once in a while (plus it degrades over time). Swapping also makes upgrades easy and feasible, like if they came up with a new version of a battery that was more efficient for example.

Swapping takes 3 mins, and is completely autonomous. You can drive up to a swap station, get out and get a coffee, it will park itself in the swapping bay, and by the time you get back with your coffee, you’ll be ready to go. For charging, you need to park, get out of the car, plug in the charger, and still wait at least another 20-30 mins and you still won’t have a full battery. Imagine on a crowded day where all chargers are used up, how long would you have to wait? This happens often in China during the Chinese new year. Autonomous swapping would also pave the way for a robo-taxi ecosystem where cars car drive itself, and swap out the batteries themselves. You can’t do that with charging (remember the awkward arm charger). 

NIO also comes with fast charging, not just battery swapping. So why would anyone not want 2 options (swapping and charging) over having only 1 (charging).

They already have the SUV side of the market covered with the model X and I know the cyber truck is technically a “truck” and not an SUV but the amount of people that will actually use it for anything truck related is pretty slim. I think if Tesla put out that roadster with anywhere near the features they promised it would have been a huge hit. The cyber truck might end up being a financial success but I think it hurt Tesla’s brand and it just doesn’t fit whatsoever in their lineup. The formula was pretty simple IMO; fast, high tech, minimalist cars with a design that appeals to the majority of people. Nothing to insane or over the top. The cyber truck is none of that and it’s become the favorite thing for YouTubers and the media to dunk on since it came out. If I’m Tesla I’m setting up an event to debut the roadster, give a realistic time frame for release and stick to the design they showed years ago. They need to give people something to talk about to get their minds off the cyber truck. I guess they’re selling a ton of them but I still think it was way too big of a change from the formula they had built a great brand using. author: @restonthewind
comment:
Even if the charger supports 250 kW, you likely won't get this rate. How many other people are charging at the same station? Most stations can't support many vehicles all charging at 250 kW even if each individual charger supports this rate. Maybe one vehicle can charge at this rate if no one else is charging. Also, the Model 3 only charges at 250 kW between ten and fifteen percent. The rate drops precipitously after fifteen percent. By fifty percent, it's below 100 kW.

Adding 175 miles in fifteen minutes is still much faster than my Bolt, but I've never had a problem with the lower rate. I only fast charge on long road trips, like over a hundred miles, and I only take a few of these trips, maybe half a dozen, in a year. So what if I spend half an hour charging, each way, on a 300 mile (each way) road trip? That's not a huge inconvenience for me, and it's the only price I pay to save ten grand or more on the price of the vehicle. If I own a Model 3, I pay for the larger battery with a faster charging rate all of the time, but I rarely use these features. If you can easily afford to do that, more power to you, but most people are more cost conscious.

comment:
It has nothing to do with charge. SOC doesn’t affect performance until 20% and below and it is visualised on the screen by showing the acceleration line turning to dots at the end. 

The reason it’s performing worse is because it’s in track mode, which prioritises longevity over performance, I.E. it limits battery overheating by keeping it as cool as possible, cooler than its optimum temperature if you are spending time idle. 

That doesn’t mean to say track mode makes the car slower, it’s just track mode expects you to be, on a track and therefore moving, thus heating up the battery, not sitting there and chatting. 

It’s as simple as that, but not well communicated in by the Tesla and while the lay person could be forgiven for not understanding this, Matty boy should know better! (Love him though)

The simplest thing that could have been done, is to use the HP to accelerate faster and not carry such a high top speed in the straights into the corners. By not over driving it, and with more acceleration, it should have easily been able to do all the laps with much better times than the previous model. comment:
I love these videos and your commentary! It is pretty incredible to see how much FSD has progressed over the years that youtubers, such as yourself, have been testing, documenting, and sharing. 

I fully believe and agree with the idea that AVs and eventually CAVs will bring a massive sea change in roadway safety. Computers are just better at handling all of this information consistently. 

One thing I urge you to consider when making your videos; adopting the tendencies of human drivers that make our roadways less safe should not be celebrated. Stop lines are painted on the ground to ensure that vehicles stop before points of conflict to ensure safety. Speed limits have been perverted to essentially becoming the speed minimum and with AVs we have an opportunity to set governors ensuring that AVs on the road are abiding by the speed limit. This is less important on interstates and other controlled access freeways (there actually might be an opportunity to *increase* the speed limits on CAFs), but it is critically important on city streets. The speed limit is 25, AVs should not be allowed to proceed faster than 25. 

Thanks again for sharing these videos and I hope you find my suggestion worthy of some sort of incorporation into your work. AVs and CAVs are the future, folks like yourself will be called on to help set policy and new rules, ensure that safety of all roads users is front of mind.

author: @theairfryermaster
comment:
These robotaxi vehicles from companies already up and running are basically just dumb machines loaded with expensive, complex sensors that scan everything around them in 360 degrees to prevent collisions, kind of like a regular robotic vacuum cleaner. But because traffic is so chaotic, mostly thanks to reckless drivers, distracted pedestrians, and annoyed cyclists, these vehicles struggle to make smart decisions in tough situations, which means they end up relying on remote human support. And that’s not a scalable solution. If you take a Waymo robotaxi outside the city, it’s all mapped out but won’t even budge.

Tesla, on the other hand, has a totally different game plan. There’s no need for those fancy LIDAR sensors; Tesla relies on computer vision and AI. As Tesla owners drive and tweak the FSD system, the AI learns how to tackle complex situations. It thinks instead of just reacting to the sensors. Just like people use their eyes to see, make sense of their surroundings, and decide based on past experiences, Tesla’s AI uses cameras to understand the world in real time and makes decisions (thinks and acts) in the smartest way for each challenge it faces.

To put it simply, Tesla’s FSD is literally LEARNING TO DRIVE like a human. Since this AI learns from data gathered from thousands of drivers, tracking and analyzing all their mistakes and wins, by 2025, it’s going to be the best and most reliable driver on the roads. Unlike humans, its calculations, decisions, and actions will occur in millionths of a second, with reaction times millions of times faster than any human. Once Tesla pulls this off, they’ll be able to roll out their self-driving cars anywhere in the world, and they’ll know how to navigate roads and highways they’ve never seen before.

So, you get why Tesla is going to totally obliterate the competition? It’s GAME OVER for everyone else.

author: @GerhardB4224
comment:
Its great entertainment but I dont know why we're still getting impressed by electric motors in a drag.  Instantaneous torque means by nature electric motors will wipe the floor in acceleration vs ICE. Racing a  fish vs a human at swimming will tell you, well, that the fish is pretty good at what its inherent design will give it an advantage in. 
The penalty of electric is weight, which  the torque can counter in a drag, but not during cornering, which this doesnt test at all.

 Hence why despite the plaid despite having twice the power and a gazillion times more torque than a GT3 RS, the 911 still laps the ring far quicker.

So it's impressive but not in a "what incredible technology"  kind of way. 

When they finally - and it will happen - make an electric that is equally as fun to drive as the other two cars on show here then that would be a true breakthrough achievement.

comment:
Thanks for the video! Additionally, this is the list of ALL changes (there are MANY):
• 4% more aerodynamic

• Fastest power folding rear seats in the industry
• Long Range is 28 lbs heavier than before
• 0.2" lower ground clearance vs old Y
• 51% less vibration on rough roads vs old Model Y, 22% overall decrease in road noise & 20% less wind noise
• 66% better call quality via improved cabin mics
• 3% stiffer body structure
• Improved braking performance for more energy recapture
• New 16 speaker sound system (up from 14 before). More punchy and much better midrange performance
• Annoying deep resonance tone from rear of car has been eliminated
• Improved door latch and door seals. More premium door "thunk" closing sound
• 27% more downforce on rear tires
• New gearing in powertrain for slight efficiency improvement
• Changed lubrication in powertrain for reduced frictional losses
• The front seats automatically move forward so the rear seat headrests don't hit the front seats when folding down

• Multicolor ambient LED interior lighting extending from dash to rear seat doors

comment:
The Core Concept: A Swappable "Skateboard" Chassis
You envision a future where the car body (the cabin, seats, and controls) is entirely separate from the "skateboard" chassis. This base unit contains all the driving components: the battery, electric motors, suspension, and wheels.
The Quick Change Charge Station
At your proposed station, the process would be incredibly fast and automated:
 * Your car body is lifted clear of its depleted base unit.
 * This depleted unit automatically moves underground for recharging and maintenance.
 * A fully charged and ready base unit rolls into place from below.
 * Your car body is then precisely lowered onto the fresh unit, establishing all necessary connections.
 * You drive away within minutes, effectively with a "full tank."
Instant Upgrades: Optional Extras on Demand
A key differentiator of your concept is the ability to instantly upgrade your vehicle's capabilities. Instead of buying a car with fixed "optional extras," you'd simply swap to a different type of base unit:
 * Need to cover long distances? Swap for a "Long Range" unit.
 * Hitting the track? Get a "Performance" unit with more powerful motors and sport-tuned suspension.
 * Going off-road? Opt for an "Off-Road" unit with higher clearance and specialized components.
This transforms traditional car ownership, allowing you to pay for performance or range only when you need it, rather than buying it upfront.
Implications
This system offers the promise of ultra-fast "refueling" and unprecedented flexibility for drivers. It could lead to lower upfront car costs as the expensive battery and drivetrain are leased or paid for on a per-use basis. Tesla would evolve into a mobility service provider, with new revenue streams from these on-demand swaps.
While incredibly innovative, such a system would require a fundamental redesign of vehicle architecture and involve immense engineering, safety, and logistical challenges for station infrastructure and managing a vast, diverse inventory of base units.

comment:
30:20 I disagree, that's a shortsighted view that ignores his claim of listening to customers while also denying the engineers their propensity to look for solutions instead of excuses not to look. 
I have a dial and at least 2 or 3 hard buttons on my Hyundai steering wheel which the computer allows each driver to configure. Each can have one of several various purposes which vary from driver to driver. They are all just inputs to the computer. Most anything you can make a control point for on the display can be also redundantly tied to a tactile switch, button, or roller so the driver can decide which control they wish to change while not distracting from full attention of surroundings. 
True, as autonomy increases the ability to focus on menus and let yourself be distracted also increases. Still, as long as there is an option to drive manually, taking away expected tactile feedbacks is a mistake.  
Even when not driving, if a radio commercial gets loud while my wife is asking a question I prefer to keep my eyes on her and reach my hand to the volume control knob I can feel and turn. If I'm driving, I can hit the mute on the steering wheel even easier.

comment: After a time I'm still uncertain about whether I like the new front versus the old more prominent headlights. I think the headlights gave it a certain personality which I liked and the thin line makes the car look less distinctive or identifiable from the front at least. I have noticed when I'm driving if I see one in the rearview mirror it's often hard to tell it from other new cars which also use the same thin line and I'm not sure that that's a good thing or a bad thing but my gut tells me it's a little better to have more distinctive lights that give the car personalities. Lights on a car have always been interpreted by your mind as the car's eyes which are very important part of any cars personality. You know the first Miata famously had its pop-up headlights which gave it a distinctive look and cars are often designed to have a friendly look on the front and a lot of that is the headlamp design. That makes them much more popular. Then you have some cars that have a hooded headlights which look a little bit like a tiger or something that is in pursuit of prey. BMW has that sort of hooded look where the sheet metal comes down over the top of the light a little bit and it makes it look like the eyes are squinting or a little meaner. author: @KaganGursoy
comment:
I had a pretty frustrating experience with my Tesla recently. When my car was around 118,000 miles, it gave me a warning that the 12V battery was going down and that I should soon go to a dealer to replace it. The message said it was safe to drive in the meantime, so I trusted that and drove a few thousand miles more, thinking I'd just have to pay a few hundred dollars to swap the 12V battery and be on my way.

To my surprise, when I finally took it in, the service team told me that the issue wasn’t actually the 12V battery—it was the main high-voltage battery that had failed. This was a complete shock, especially since the car only warned me about the 12V battery and clearly stated it was safe to keep driving. Now I’m being told the entire battery pack needs to be replaced, which costs over $15,000.

Even worse, I’m now just slightly over the 120,000-mile battery warranty—by only a few thousand miles. Had I known the real issue was the main battery, I would’ve brought the car in immediately and stayed within the warranty. But because of the misleading warning, I unknowingly missed that window.

I’ve always admired Tesla for its innovation, but this experience has really shaken my trust. I’m hoping Tesla will do the right thing—whether by honoring the warranty or offering some kind of assistance. It doesn’t feel right for a loyal customer to be hit with such a massive repair bill due to unclear communication from the vehicle.

comment:
For the auto reversing and gear shift, I’d say I rely on that 9 time out of 10. Paul obviously wasn’t familiar with it, but the Tesla doesn’t just change gears willy nilly on you.  It’s smarter than that, and is expecting certain conditions. For example, you hardly want your car by default automatically engaging reverse whenever you approach a barrier, otherwise it will go into reverse each time you park. However it will detect things like a three point turn quiet well, or if your parallel parking, it works well to detect that you’ve pulled in and backed up to the car behind you, and sensibly changes gears after you push the brake to finish the manoeuvre , while telling you what it’s about to do. 

The system works remarkably well (not perfectly), I think Paul just needs to be familiar with it.
